meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas (live data, not an archived version; give corpus_snapshot and source_commit). doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.mechanism: Rapamycin extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice even when started late in life - one of the most influential results in the geroscience arm of this Atlas.
data.mechanism_beginner: Rapamycin makes mice live longer, even when given late in life – the single biggest result behind the whole "this pathway and ageing" idea.
data.boundary: The lifespan result is mouse only. No human lifespan or healthspan trial is held in this corpus and EVERLAST has no results yet; the closest human survival data here, STE2026, is observational, at immunosuppressive doses in kidney transplant recipients, and found no benefit, which is why it sits on this edge as a conflicting study rather than as support. BIT2016 shows a non-continuous schedule can still extend post-treatment life expectancy, but the result is dose- and route-specific: in the 8 mg/kg/day intraperitoneal arm males gained +60% post-treatment life expectancy (p=0.02) while females showed no survival benefit (p=0.261) and a shift toward aggressive haematopoietic cancers (16/16 vs 6/12, p=0.002); in the same paper's 126 ppm dietary encapsulated-rapamycin arm survival rose significantly in BOTH sexes, with a Cox model finding no evidence that sex modified the treatment effect (p=0.904). Cite the arm, not just the paper. ARR2016: an intermittent regimen (2 mg/kg every 5 days) started as late as 20 months of age extended lifespan in female C57BL/6J mice; the abstract reports the effect in females only.

conflict.basis: The lifespan evidence on this edge is mouse, at low or intermittent doses, in healthy animals (HAR2009, BIT2016, ARR2016). STE2026 is human: in a US registry of 11,474 kidney transplant recipients alive at one year, rapamycin at immunosuppressive doses alongside other immunosuppressants gave no survival benefit (median survival age 64.6 against 64.3 years, 95% CI for the difference -1.6 to 2.0). Different species, dose, population and endpoint, so it bounds the human reach of the claim rather than reversing the mouse result.

data.note: ARR2015 was removed from this edge on 2026-07-29: that study measured side effects only and has no survival endpoint. 2026-11-07: STE2026 recorded as a conflicting study, human registry survival data at immunosuppressive doses, which bounds how far the mouse result reaches into people; the boundary no longer says that no human endpoint exists at all.
